data.title: Rohingya crisis remains unresolved as ICJ rules on Myanmar
data.description:
A long-awaited judgment from the UN's highest court on Thursday said that killings, destruction of homes and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar's security forces amounted to state-sponsored genocide of the Rohingya Muslim minority population.

The decision comes nearly a decade after a 2017 military crackdown drove more than 730,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh, and as conflict, shrinking humanitarian aid and dangerous sea crossings continue to leave many members of the community displaced and vulnerable.

WHY DID THE ROHINGYA FLEE MYANMAR?

More than 1.3 million Rohingya remain displaced across South and Southeast Asia, including 1.2 million in sprawling refugee camps in Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh, according to the United Nations.

The largest displacement began in August 2017, when Myanmar's armed forces launched an offensive following attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army insurgent group on about 30 police posts and an army base.

The military crackdown forced hundreds of thousands of Rohingya to flee into Bangladesh. Refugees described mass killings, gang rapes, torture and the burning of hundreds of villages, according to Human Rights Watch.

Myanmar's government denied the allegations, saying its forces were targeting militants.

WHAT IS THE ICJ CASE AGAINST MYANMAR?

In 2019, Gambia filed a case at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), also known as the World Court, backed by the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, alleging that Myanmar's 2017 military offensive in Rakhine State amounted to genocide.

The ICJ judgments are final and binding, but the court has limited means of enforcement and cannot convict individuals or issue arrest warrants.

In 2019 preliminary hearings in the ICJ case, Myanmar's then leader, Aung San Suu Kyi, rejected Gambia's accusations of genocide as "incomplete and misleading".

The ICJ in January 2020 ordered Myanmar to take urgent measures to protect Rohingya people remaining in the country, including preventing possible genocidal acts and preserving evidence.

WHAT IS THE SITUATION IN RAKHINE?

Myanmar's military, led by Min Aung Hlaing, seized power in February 2021. The overthrow of Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government triggered a nationwide civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.

As conflict spread, renewed fighting between Myanmar's military junta and the Arakan Army rebel group broke out in Rakhine State in November 2023, forcing more Rohingya civilians to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh.

The minority group has also faced attacks by the Arakan Army, which set alight swathes of the Rohingya settlement of Buthidaung in May 2024, Reuters has reported.

WHY CAN'T THE ROHINGYA RETURN?

As conflict rages on in Rakhine, conditions for the safe return of Rohingya refugees do not currently exist, according to aid groups.

Myanmar said in August that it had verified 308,797 people living in displacement camps in Bangladesh as former residents of Rakhine State, but repatriation would begin only when security conditions in Rakhine improve.

Some Rohingya refugees say they are not willing to go back without full rights, dignity, and citizenship.

Myanmar's government has long seen the Rohingya as illegal migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh and denied them citizenship, even though Rohingya families have lived in Myanmar for generations.

Earlier repatriation plans in 2018 and 2019 resulted in no returns.

data.title: US shale companies send oil windfall to shareholders as prices jump
data.description:
Key points:
  • US shale producers are boosting shareholder returns at a faster pace than global oil majors
  • Buybacks and dividends up 41% year-on-year during Q3
  • Analysts say independent producers favor buybacks; majors maintained returns
  • Output growth remains muted despite higher crude prices
  • ConocoPhillips, Devon and APA signal further shareholder returns

By Katha Kalia and Vallari Srivastava

US shale producers are returning the windfall from surging oil prices to shareholders at a faster pace than global majors, with the group's buybacks and dividends rising 41% during the third quarter, from a year earlier.

Brent crude has risen more than 50% in 2026 amid supply disruptions caused by the Middle East conflict, making it one of the most profitable periods for the oil and gas sector in recent years.

Devon Energy , ConocoPhillips , Diamondback Energy , Occidental Petroleum , APA and EOG said in their third-quarter results they would prioritize shareholder returns while forecasting only modest production growth next year.

Combined, the six companies returned about $7.25 billion through dividends and buybacks in the quarter, roughly $2.11 billion more than a year earlier, according to Reuters calculation.

In contrast, larger rivals Exxon Mobil and Chevron did not increase shareholder returns, maintaining them at $9.4 billion and nearly $6 billion, respectively.

"Supermajors focused this quarter on allocating high profits towards reducing debt," said Rystad Energy's Matthew Bernstein. Geographic and revenue diversification enables them to confidently fund existing capital plans and shareholder return frameworks, with oil-price related cash influx going towards reducing debt, Bernstein said.

ConocoPhillips said buybacks would increase in the fourth quarter and it aims to return 45% of cash flow from operations to shareholders in 2027.

Devon expects buybacks to step up to over $1 billion in the current quarter and rise further in 2027. APA expects to repurchase an additional $650 million of shares by year-end and, along with dividends, is on track to return at least 60% of annual free cash flow to shareholders.

Melius Research analyst James West expects buybacks to continue, though he suggests companies could boost output if the Middle East conflict ends and oil stays above $80 a barrel.

During the third-quarter, Diamondback increased its dividend by 7%, while EOG and ConocoPhillips raised by 8% and 11%, respectively.

Exxon plans to maintain annual share repurchases at $20 billion in 2027, CEO Darren Woods said on the earnings call, adding that the oil major prioritizes "certainty" and "reliability" in shareholder distributions while avoiding "over-exuberant" spending during periods of high commodity prices.

"The majors set a dollar amount for their buyback programs and hold to it. The independents tend to adjust their buyback activity based on their current cash flows," Jeff Krimmel, founder of consulting firm Krimmel Strategy, said.

PRODUCTION GROWTH RESTRAINED

Diamondback CEO Kaes Van't Hof said oil prices have been "all over the place throughout this year." Brent crude has traded as low as $59.75 per barrel and as high as $126.41 per barrel in a period of just nine months.

"So our best protection is to keep that reinvestment rate low, generate a ton of free cash and then allocate that free cash appropriately," Van't Hof said on the earnings call.

Diamondback's reinvestment rate, which refers to the ratio between capital expenditure and cash flow from operations, stood at 32% during the third quarter, compared with 36%-37% a year earlier.

Diamondback, EOG, ConocoPhillips and Devon forecast a low single-digit increase in production in 2027. Occidental expects flat production next year, while APA forecast similar volumes in US and Egypt year-over-year.

"In past cycles, oil in mid-$80s would have pulled exploration and production budgets higher within a quarter or two," Melius' West said in a research note, adding that US shale producers spent roughly what they had budgeted at the start of the year.

data.title: Stock Futures Rise Ahead of Anthropic Trading Debut — Update
data.description:
By Joe Stonor

Nasdaq futures led a rally in U.S. stocks premarket, after Anthropic's pricing of its hotly anticipated listing lifted confidence around the artificial-intelligence trade.

The expectation-beating IPO pricing of the company behind the Claude chatbot helped investor focus shift away from the AI jitters that have weighed on stocks so far this week. However, sentiment was tempered by hawkish Federal Reserve meeting minutes Wednesday that added to fears of extended policy tightening.

Nasdaq futures jumped 2% as chip makers and cloud-computing stocks rallied premarket. Anthropic sold more shares at a higher price than anticipated, implying a value of around $1.5 trillion for the company. S&P 500 futures were also in the green--up 1.2%--as the index looks to turn the tide on a fifth-straight day of losses. Contracts tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.6%. The index has fallen by more than 1% for three days in a row.

Equities were mixed across Asia, where the tech-dominated Nikkei Stock Average in Japan and South Korea's Kospi closed in the green. Stock indexes in Hong Kong and Shanghai fell, however. In Europe, major indexes were mixed as the continent-wide Stoxx 600 slipped 0.1%.

Treasury yields ticked higher after falling in Asian trade, as investors respond to a hawkish readout from the Fed's October meeting. Near-term rate-sensitive two-year yields rose above 4.800%, while 10-year yields nudged back toward 5.100%. Thirty-year yields hovered around 5.440%.

Oil prices rose, picking up from falls Wednesday after U.S. crude oil inventories rose for a second consecutive week. The benchmark Brent crude contract rose 1% to trade around $93 a barrel, while the West Texas Intermediate contract nudged up 0.9% to trade around $84 a barrel.

The dollar fell slightly, but remained close to its highest level against a basket of global currencies since January 2025. Copper prices steadied after falling sharply in the last session but gold extended losses, trading close to $3,700 a troy ounce. Bitcoin rallied after recent declines, adding over 2% to trade around $63,750.

Anthropic's trading debut will be in focus for the day ahead. Investors will also watch for readouts from the trilateral meeting between President Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen.

data.title: Indian lender Yes Bank's AT-1 bond investors urge RBI to focus on investor protection
data.description:
By Jayshree P Upadhyay and Arpan Chaturvedi

Holders of Indian private-sector lender Yes Bank's AT-1 bonds have written to the country's central bank urging it to prioritise investor protection after it sought a review of a Supreme Court ruling that restored these bonds last month, according to a copy of the letter reviewed by Reuters.

The dispute stems from Yes Bank's rescue in 2020, when authorities wrote off 84.15 billion rupees worth of additional Tier-1 (AT1) bonds, a type of security designed to absorb losses when banks run into trouble.

Last month, the Supreme Court ruled the write-off illegal over procedural lapses and ordered the bonds restored, but review petitions by the bank and the Reserve Bank of India have delayed relief for investors.

Bondholders in their letter dated November 18 said the RBI has remained "absent" in its capacity as the regulator "responsible for protecting the interests of the investing public and the integrity of the banking system."

Acting on behalf of the bondholders, Axis Trustee Services Limited has separately filed a contempt petition in the Supreme Court alleging Yes Bank and its directors have failed to comply with court directions and have not taken any steps to restore the bonds.

In the contempt petition, a copy of which has been reviewed by Reuters, the trustee said bondholders, including retail investors, pension funds and provident funds, had been deprived of their investments for more than six years and still have no visibility on restoration of the bonds and payment of coupons.

The trustee argued that the bank could not avoid complying with the ruling while pursuing other legal remedies because the judgment remained in force.

The bondholders in their letter to the central bank said they expect the RBI to oversee implementation of the Supreme Court verdict and to protect investors rather than align itself with further challenges to the ruling.

The RBI and Yes Bank did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

data.title: US energy chief Wright sees no sign Europe wants return to Russia energy
data.description:
US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said on Thursday he sees no sign of any European country being interested in renewing Russian energy imports when asked about media reports of alleged US plans to facilitate Russian gas sales to Europe.

"The nations of Europe have spoken loud and clear. They bet their energy future on Russia, not just for natural gas, but for oil and coal as well, that bet did not go well. I have not heard a single European nation interested in reengaging in energy imports from Russia," told a news conference at the Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation in Warsaw.

Reuters reported last month that top Russian and US officials, including US Special Envoy Jared Kushner, had held talks about bringing a US investor into the Nord Stream pipelines that delivered gas to Europe via Germany before Russia invaded Ukraine, Reuters reported last month.

The Nord Stream gas pipelines are currently sanctioned by the US and the EU making any restart illegal, but potential US ownership could prompt Washington to soften its stance.

"No, I can't confirm that. I read all sorts of things in the press and I will tell you, all sorts of ideas are thrown around," Wright said.

Wright's comments come as the unprecedented meeting of leaders of United States, China and Russian exposed differences over Ukraine even as a "peace declaration" was agreed.

The European Union has been phasing out Russian energy since Moscow started its war in Ukraine in 2022. It plans to halt all liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports by the end of 2026 and all pipeline gas imports by late 2027.

Polish energy firm Orlen on Wednesday signed agreements on potential supply of LNG to Hungary and Slovakia, among the EU member countries most impacted by the EU's phase-out plans.

US President Donald Trump announced a surprise deal with Moscow to import diesel from Russia to help lower prices at the pumps ahead of this month's US midterm elections. No deliveries have yet been made.

"Regarding Russian energy deals, I can't say anything about the future after the war."

data.title: Walmart Sales Rise Powered by E-Commerce Gains — WSJ
data.description:
By Sarah Nassauer

Walmart is moving further away from relying on store sales.

On Thursday, Walmart said its sales and profits from e-commerce, advertising and other newer businesses were growing, while its store sales continued to slide.

It is a shift in how Walmart operates after starting as a discount retailer in 1962. The bulk of the chain's sales and profits still comes from U.S. stores, but that will keep changing, the company said.

Overall, Walmart's total revenue grew 5.2% to $188.8 billion in the three months ended Oct. 31. Based on its sales performance, Walmart raised its guidance for the full year.

The company has been doubling down on e-commerce in recent years, working to speed delivery and offer a wider range of products from third-party sellers to stoke sales.

More Americans now shop online. Walmart has been among the legacy bricks-and-mortar retailers most aggressively ramping up their online operations to get ahead of the shoppers' shift and fend off Amazon.com.

Amazon surpassed Walmart as America's biggest company by revenue earlier this year.

Walmart U.S. comparable sales, those from both stores and digital channels operating at least 12 months, grew 2.9% in the three months ended Oct 30. That is slightly higher than the 2.6% growth it reported the previous quarter, its slowest growth in six years.

Walmart didn't break out store-specific or e-commerce sales results. Chief Financial Officer John David Rainey said its U.S. store comparables fell in the most recent quarter, though he said the figure is less meaningful than it has been because stores help fulfill a large chunk of e-commerce sales.

"Stores and, I would argue, our delivery networks are actually becoming digital assets," Rainey said. "If you just focus on the in-store comp, that really misses what's going on in our business."

Its most recent U.S. sales figure was helped by market-share gains in its food business and hurt by pricing regulation in its pharmacy business, without which comparable sales would have been 3.6%, said the company.

Walmart's market-share gains in food were the largest in three years, said Rainey, as the company worked to decrease prices. Thanks to lower prices, Walmart has sold a million more turkeys than last year at this point in the Thanksgiving season, he said.

Yet its strongest growth came from its e-commerce, membership and advertising businesses. Its global e-commerce sales grew by 17% and 23% in the U.S. Its U.S. advertising business was up 37%.

"Our multiyear growth in e-commerce is evidence that customers are choosing Walmart because we deliver price, speed, and convenience across a broad assortment," said Walmart Chief Executive John Furner.

For the quarter, Walmart's adjusted earnings per share grew 4.8% to $0.65, above analysts expectations for $0.64.

It now expects earnings per share to hit $2.84 to $2.89, up from a previous range of $2.80 to $2.87. It also expects net sales to grow 4.9% to 5.2%, up from a previous range of 4% to 5%.

data.title: Canadian Oil Exports Rise, Feeding Asia Demand — Market Talk
data.description: RBC Capital Markets analysis shows that 30 oil tankers departed from Canada's Westridge Marine Terminal in October, the highest tanker count observed and up by six from September. It estimates export volumes climbed to 15.9 million barrels, rebounding from the prior month's downturn. Asia-Pacific was again the main destination for tankers last month, and RBC says China received the bulk of shipments. This persistent draw from Asian buyers on Canadian tidewater barrels, coupled with anticipated oil-supply growth from Alberta's efforts to grow oil sands output, reinforces the case for incremental outbound flows from the west coast.
